results.title: Pretest with Caution: Event-Study Estimates after Testing for Parallel Trends | Request PDF
results.content: An emerging research literature has cautioned against the use of pre-tests for violations of parallel trends in the pre-treatment period altogether as they may have adverse effects on classical DID inference, such as bias and severe undercovarage (Bilinski and Hatfield, 2020;Kahn-Lang and Lang, 2020;Freyaldenhoven, Hansen, and Shapiro, 2019;Roth, 2022). Because there is no treatment in the placebo periods and anticipatory effects are ruled out by assumption, any measured pre-testing effect is the result of a parallel trends violation (Roth, 2022;Rambachan and Roth, 2023). We evaluate the robustness of our event-study estimates and timing of the policy effects (if they exist) using the method proposed in Roth (2022). The main idea is to re-estimate the treatment effects given the largest potential bias unconditional on passing the pre-trend test, which lends further support to the causal interpretation of our results. However, conducting statistical pre-trend tests and conditioning the analysis on passing these tests may exacerbate bias in the estimated treatment effects because the observed draws of data that pass such tests are a select sample from the true underlying data-generating process [76]. Taken together, the alignment across the baseline specification, the power analysis using Roth (2022), the robust inference framework of Rambachan and Roth (2023), and this adjusted model with an explicit pre-trend term provide strong evidence that differential pre-trends are unlikely to be driving the estimated effects of NRCMS. The core identification strategy of this study relies on a multi-period DID framework, the validity of which depends critically on the parallel trends assumption-i.e., that treatment and control groups would have followed similar trajectories in the absence of policy intervention (Callaway, 2021;Roth, 2022). The assumption of parallel trends suggests that before the implementation of the policy, both the treatment and control groups follow a common trend, which serves as a fundamental prerequisite for obtaining unbiased estimations and accurately identifying causality through the traditional DID method (Roth 2022). In this article, we consider identification, estimation, and inference procedures for treatment effect parameters using Difference-in-Differences (DiD) with (i) multiple time periods, (ii) variation in treatment timing, and (iii) when the “parallel trends assumption” holds potentially only after conditioning on observed covariates.
